titleStmt.title: History of the Zhou Dynasty · Western Zhou 西周

div.head: c. 1046–1036 BC
div.p: After Di Xin's death, King Wu's next step was to bring the royal domain of Yin Shang wholly under his control; according to the Yi Zhou Shu, King Wu, after entering Zhaoge on the evening of the day Jiazi, at once sent Taigong with an army to hold off Fang Lai, a minister of Di Xin. Three days later, on the day Dingmao, Taigong came back victorious, having for the most part put out what resistance remained in the royal domain of Yin Shang.

In the royal domain of Yinxu, apart from Fang Lai and the other remnants of resistance, the kinsmen and old clans of Yin Shang for the most part had no heart to stand against the Zhou army; according to the Zuozhuan, Weizi Qi, Di Xin's elder brother by a secondary consort, came of his own accord to offer his surrender to King Wu, and King Wu with his own hands loosed Weizi Qi's bonds, accepted the jade disc he held in his mouth, and then ordered him back to his fief, the land of Wei (微).

By the account of the Yi Zhou Shu, Conquest of Yin, King Wu held a sacrifice at the altar of the soil in the royal domain of Yin Shang, enfeoffed Wu Geng, Di Xin's son, at the settlement of Yin, and ordered his third brother Guanshu Xian to assist him; King Wu sent the Duke of Shao to release the imprisoned Jizi, sent Bishu and Kangshu to release the kinsmen whom Di Xin had imprisoned, and ordered Hong Yao to raise a mound over the tomb of Bigan. King Wu summoned the nobles great and small of the royal domain of Yin Shang to meet him outside the settlement of Yin, and delivered an admonition to them, which is the Speech to Shang.

The inscription of the Li gui, a Western Zhou bronze unearthed at Lintong in Shaanxi, shows that on the day Xinwei, that is, seven days after the conquest of Shang, King Wu had already left the royal domain of Yin Shang and reached Lanshi; according to the Yi Zhou Shu, Great Capture, King Wu ordered Lü Ta to campaign against the Yuexifang, Hou Lai to attack Miji in the land of Chen, Bai Yan to attack Wei (韦), Chen Ben to attack Li (磿), Bai Wei to attack the Xuanfang and Xin Huang to attack Shu, and all six columns were victorious. After these victories King Wu led his army back to Haojing, and on Gengxu of April held the rite of presenting the captives. On the day Xinhai he sacrificed to Heaven, and with this the war against Zhou (纣) was complete.

King Wu's rule after the conquest of Shang was fairly short, three years at the most. In this time King Wu made enfeoffments to the "descendants of the former dynasties" and to his kinsmen and ministers of merit.

Among the "descendants of the former dynasties", the descendants of the royal houses of the two dynasties of Xia and Yin, three states in all, were enfeoffed, and are together called the "Three Ke"; of these "Three Ke" the "descendants of Shun" are the state of Chen, the "descendants of Xia" the state of Qi (杞), and as for the "descendants of Yin", they were at first Wu Geng, Di Xin's son, enfeoffed at Bei. Later, when Wu Geng rose in revolt and was put down, the Duke of Zhou ordered Weizi Qi, Di Xin's elder brother by a secondary consort, to "take the place of the descendants of Yin", and the state of Song thus became one of the "Three Ke". Besides these, others too were enfeoffed, such as the descendants of Yandi and the Yellow Emperor, the descendants of Yao and others.

Besides Guanshu Xian, sent at the very beginning of the conquest of Shang to assist Wu Geng, King Wu also sent two more of his full brothers, Caishu Du and Huoshu Chu, setting up the "Three Guards" to keep watch over the people of Yin, and divided up the royal domain of Yin Shang; King Wu of Zhou also enfeoffed several of his full brothers at Cao, Gao, Cheng (郕) and other places, and enfeoffed Taigong, Lü Shang, at Yingqiu, who put down the Laiyi and founded the state of Qi (齐), gaining a foothold in the eastern lands.

By the beginning of Zhou, people of the Jiang surname had moved in numbers into the middle and upper reaches of Jing River, and lived side by side with Zhou people from the heart of the Western Zhou royal domain in the districts of Lingtai, Chongxin, Ning County, Heshui and Huan County in Gansu, on the main stream of Jing River and its tributary Malian River.

After King Wu's death his son King Cheng came to the throne, and Ji Dan, Duke of Zhou, on King Wu's dying charge, "conducted the affairs of the Son of Heaven in his stead", issuing all his orders as "the King's command"; Guanshu and Caishu, who were then in the east overseeing the people of Yin, were greatly displeased, and at once set themselves against him.

As for Huoshu, some scholars think he may only have been carried along by his two elder brothers and was not a chief mover of the troubles, which is why the early texts for the most part pass him over; as Guan and Cai openly set themselves against the Duke of Zhou, Wu Geng, Di Xin's son, also raised troops at the settlement of Yin.

The traditional accounts for the most part hold that Guan and Cai rose in revolt in league with Wu Geng, but some scholars infer from the record of the Xinian of the Tsinghua slips that Guan and Cai at first perhaps simply opposed the Duke of Zhou and were not in collusion with Wu Geng; the nobles and remnant people of the former royal domain of Yin Shang, seeing the royal house of Zhou at strife within itself, killed the Zhou officers and soldiers left at the settlement of Yin and raised Wu Geng in revolt.
According to the Shangshu Dazhuan, the rulers of the state of Yan (奄) and of Pugu also sent men to tell Wu Geng to rise.

Guan and Cai gave out that "the Duke will do no good to the young son", so that the other great ministers of the Zhou court, and even King Cheng himself, came to doubt the Duke of Zhou's regency; the Duke of Zhou on the one hand did his utmost to set out the pains he had taken, and on the other made it plain that he would show no indulgence to those who raised revolt.

The first year of the Duke of Zhou's eastern campaign was spent mainly in checking the offensive of Guan, Cai and the old clans of Yin Shang; the Duke of Zhou held the land of Luo in person, while his son Boqin led an army in behind Guanshu's fief, and the other rulers of states and Lords also acted in concert with the Duke of Zhou: the two states of Wen and Tan held the main road running south from the royal domain of Yin Shang to the region of Yi River and Luo River, the two states of Yuan and Yong held the Passes at the southern foot of Taihangshan, and the Ji-surnamed state of Li (黎) guarded the Shangdang Plateau on the western side of Taihangshan; under their blockade the rebel army of the royal domain of Yin Shang could do nothing.

Along Ji River, the states that the Zhou army's earlier advance to the east had produced, Qi (齐), Cheng (郕), Cao, Gao and others, moreover pinned down the pro-Shang fang states, of which the state of Yan (奄) and Pugu were the chief, so that they could give no effective support to the royal domain of Yin Shang.

In the second year of the eastern campaign the Duke of Zhou utterly defeated Guan and Cai; Guanshu was either put to death or killed himself, and Caishu was either imprisoned or banished together with Huoshu.

After the defeat and ruin of Guan and Cai, the Duke of Zhou went on to lead his army against the settlement of Yin and took it, and Wu Geng fled north; from the charred posts and the burnt red earth of the foundations found in the excavations at Xiaotun, Anyang, it can be known that the capital of Yin went through a fire when it was finally abandoned. The royal tombs of Yinxu, and the great majority of the nobles' tombs outside the royal cemetery, were also plundered and wrecked together in the course of the Duke of Zhou's eastern campaign, and Late Shang Yinxu Phase IV came to a final end.

Once King Cheng's misunderstanding of the Duke of Zhou was cleared away, in the third year of the eastern campaign he took part in person in the great campaign of the "trampling of Yan (奄)". On the other side, King Cheng sent the Grand Guardian Shi, Duke of Shao, with an army against Wu Geng, who had fled north; although Wu Geng was overtaken and killed, a part of his following still fled on northwards, and the Duke of Shao pursued them with his army as far as the land of Yan (燕), where he set up strongholds. Afterwards, when the Duke of Shao brought his army home, King Cheng enfeoffed the Duke of Shao's son Ke as Marquis of Yan (匽).

Before this there was already in the Beijing region the state of Ji (㠱), founded by Jizi's clan after its move north; to judge from the excavated inscriptions in which the Marquis of Yan (匽) makes gifts to kinsmen of the Marquis of Ji (㠱), this branch of the remnant people of Yin Shang was on fairly good terms with the state of Yan (匽); as for the remnants of Wu Geng's revolt, they perhaps fled to somewhere a little further north, for example the state of Guzhu, and the vessels of Yin Shang type among the remains of western Liaoning at the beginning of the Western Zhou may have to do with them.

After the state of Yan (奄) was broken, Feilian, a minister of Di Xin who had taken refuge there, fled on eastwards, and the Zhou army pursued him to the edge of the sea and killed him; King Cheng also moved the remnant people of the state of Yan (奄), Feilian's kinsmen among them, west to Zhuyushan, and ordered them to hold off the "Rong of Nucuo".

After destroying the state of Yan (奄), the Duke of Zhou also led his army against the Dongyi state of the Earl of Feng and the state of Pugu; these two states must have been destroyed with Taigong's cooperation, which is why both were afterwards added by King Cheng to the fief of the state of Qi (齐). After this the Duke of Zhou campaigned widely against the southern states.

After the fall of the several chief pro-Shang fang states, Ji (纪), Xue and other states of the east also went over to the Zhou people; according to the Yi Zhou Shu, the Duke of Zhou also conquered "seventeen states of the Xiong and Ying clans" of the Dongyi; the great Dongyi state of Xu (徐), however, seems not to have been badly hurt, and later, when the Duke of Zhou's son Boqin was moved to a fief in the east, he still had to fight the state of Xu (徐).

After the victory of the eastern campaign, the Duke of Zhou moved a body of the old nobility of Yin Shang who had raised Wu Geng in revolt to Jiubi, that is, near the land of Luo, where a strong force was stationed, so that once the new capital Luoyi was built they could be controlled from close at hand; because they had earlier resisted the rule of the Zhou people, they are also called the "refractory people".

In the fifth year of his regency the Duke of Zhou built Chengzhou, Luoyi, after which still more of the old clans of Yin Shang were moved and settled near it. The Duke of Zhou also restated his policy of conciliation, by which men of virtue would be chosen to serve at the royal court, while the other people of Yin moved to Luoyi could also be given fields.

Besides Chengzhou, Luoyi, some of the old clans of Yin Shang were also moved and settled in the Zhouyuan and at Feng and Hao; unlike the "refractory people" of Luoyi, these old clans were for the most part the party willing to work with the Zhou people, and as early as the beginning of King Wu's conquest of Shang they were moved one after another to the western lands.

As for the royal domain of Yin Shang, many remnant people who had not been moved were still there. The Duke of Zhou had his full brother Kangshu Feng govern the remnant people of Yin Shang who stayed where they were, and after King Cheng took up the government himself he commended Kangshu's services and called him back to court to serve as Minister of Justice.

Much as in the royal domain of Yin Shang, in the old land of Shang Yan (商奄), after a body of "refractory people" had later been moved away, many remnant people still stayed where they were, and so Boqin was ordered to move to the east to make fast the fruits of the Duke of Zhou's eastern campaign. Near the capital of the state of Xu (许), however, there still remained Xutian, an "exclave" of the state of Lu, as a lodging for the rulers of Lu when they went to Luo to attend court.

div.head: c. 1046–1036 BC: archaeological appearances
div.p: c. the beginning of the Western Zhou:

The Upper Xiajiadian culture took over from the Gaotaishan culture and carried its development forward; the Shi'ertaiyingzi culture took over from the Weiyingzi culture and carried its development forward.
The bronze cultures of the north in the Zhou period passed by degrees into a blank period; the Baode type took over from the Shilou type and carried its development forward.
The Siwa culture entered the second stage of its middle period, and as it developed the Lanqiao–Xujianian type took shape within it.
The Xituanshan, Baoshan and Tanheli cultures and the Wanfabozi remains arose.

div.head: c. 1036–1000 BC
div.p: In the seventh year of his regency the Duke of Zhou gave the government back to King Cheng; after his death he was buried at Bi.

King Cheng's full brother Tangshu Yu was likewise enfeoffed, at Yang; after Shuyu's death his son Xiefu succeeded him, and in the twenty-eighth year of King Cheng moved from the land of Tang to the land of Jin.

Archaeology shows that the state of Yan of the first years of the Western Zhou, once it had a firm footing in the Beijing region, went on to try to extend its power into western Liaoning; an early Western Zhou bronze yu was once unearthed at Machanggou village, Kazuo, in Liaoning.

King Cheng died, and the Heir Apparent Zhao succeeded to the throne. In the growth of the Zhou dynasty King Wen and King Kang did a good deal that stands out, and their contribution was marked; in his eastern campaign the Duke of Zhou had campaigned against the Dongyi but had not destroyed them, and so in the time of King Kang of Zhou there was again a war against the Dongyi, who had risen in revolt, which was carried right to the edge of the sea, and the eastern states were attacked as well; it is not known what the state of Chu did in King Kang's time to turn against Zhou, but in King Kang's time there was the war of the "attack on the Earl of Chu", and also a campaign against the Hufang.

Sima Qian's Shiji, Basic Annals of Zhou says: "In the time of Cheng and Kang all under Heaven was at peace, and the punishments were laid aside, unused for more than forty years." Later ages all call the period of the rule of King Cheng and King Kang the "Good Governance of Cheng and Kang".

div.head: c. 1000–950 BC
div.p: After King Kang of Zhou's death his son Xia succeeded to the throne; he is King Zhao. The wars of King Zhao's time were mainly the southern campaigns; set side by side, the transmitted texts and the inscriptions agree in the main, and there are also things the texts never mention, such as the attacks on the Dongyi, Kuai and others.

In his sixteenth year King Zhao attacked the rebellious Jing, as archaeological finds bear out; the inscription of the Guo Bo gui says: "The Earl of Guo followed the King in attacking the rebellious Jing and took metal; with it he made this treasured sacrificial vessel for the ancestral hall." King Zhao's war against Jing in his nineteenth year was probably more terrible than that of the sixteenth; according to the old-text Bamboo Annals, the six armies under King Zhao's command were also disastrously beaten, which it puts as "the six armies perished in the Han."

After King Zhao's death his son Man succeeded to the throne; he is King Mu. What the Shiji, Basic Annals of Zhou says of King Mu of the Western Zhou is a little fuller than for the two kings Kang and Zhao, but still very brief. As to war, it has only the campaign against the Quan Rong; the record of the old-text Bamboo Annals is fuller.

The Mu Tianzi Zhuan, unearthed under the Western Jin, also tells the story of King Mu of Zhou setting out from Luoyi and, after passing through various tribes and states, meeting the Queen Mother of the West.

From the early part of King Mu's reign the Huaiyi began to be a great danger to the Zhou in the south-east; in the inscriptions of the excavated bronzes of King Mu's period records of resisting the Huaiyi begin to appear often, and the lines of Ru River, Ying River and Sha River were all subject to their raids.

In the inscriptions of the excavated bronzes of King Mu's period there are also records of "holding off the Nanyi" (戍南夷); the 戍 of the inscriptions has the sense of checking or holding off, which differs from the sense of garrisoning, and so "holding off the Nanyi" in itself shows that this was war, and a war distinct from the resistance to the Huaiyi.

div.head: c. 1000–950 BC: archaeological appearances
div.p: The Xindian culture entered its final period; the Kayue culture entered its Phase V.
The Upper Misong-ri culture took over from the Sinam-ri Phase II culture and carried its development forward.
The Geumtan-ri Bronze Age culture entered its Phase II.

div.head: c. 950–900 BC
div.p: In his later years King Mu attacked the Huaiyi and the eastern states, as archaeological finds bear witness; the inscription of the Ban gui says: "In three years he brought peace to the eastern states, and none did not submit." Another inscription shows that at this time the Huaiyi invaded the interior, and King Mu ordered Dong to take the field, and he fought them at the state of Hu.

According to the excavated Da Yu ding and Xiao Yu ding, in King Mu's time there are also records of Yu twice campaigning against the Guifang at the King's command; the very first campaign against the Guifang brought great gains: three chiefs of the Guifang were captured, the ears of more than four thousand eight hundred men were cut off, more than thirteen thousand men were taken prisoner, with thirty chariots and more than three hundred oxen, and on his return the rite of presenting the captives was held.

After King Mu's death his son Yihu was set on the throne; he is King Gong. So far as is known at present, no vessel inscription recording war that belongs to King Gong's reign has yet been found; some vessel inscriptions that record war cannot be assigned with certainty to King Gong, King Yi (懿) or King Xiao, and can only be placed for the time being under the "middle Western Zhou".
As to the wars of King Gong's time, all that the transmitted texts record is King Gong's destruction of Mi, in Sima Qian's Shiji, Basic Annals of Zhou.
After King Gong's death his son Jian succeeded; he is King Yi (懿).

div.head: c. 900–860 BC
div.p: In the time of King Yi (懿) the royal house thereupon declined, and the Rong and Di invaded in turn and ravaged the central states.

According to the Shi Mi gui, an excavated object of King Yi (懿)'s period, because the Nanyi "widely attacked the eastern states", the King ordered Shi Su and Shi Mi to lead the army of the state of Qi to punish them.
Huaili in Right Fufeng was called Quanqiu under the Zhou; King Yi (懿) made it his capital.
After King Yi (懿) of Zhou's death, Pifang, younger brother of King Gong, succeeded; he is King Xiao.

According to the Shiji, Basic Annals of Qin, Feizi of Qin, a man of Quanqiu, won the favour of King Xiao of Zhou by his skill in rearing horses, and the King "gave him Qin as his settlement, had him take up again the sacrifices of the Ying clan, and styled him Qin Ying."
After King Xiao of Zhou's death the Lords in turn set up Xie, the Heir Apparent of King Yi (懿); he is King Yi (夷).

According to the Shiji, Hereditary House of Chu, the state of Chu set itself up as a kingdom after King Yi (夷) came to the throne, and gave up the royal title only in the time of King Li; the commentary to the Hou Hanshu, Account of the Western Qiang also quotes the Bamboo Annals for King Yi (夷) ordering the Duke of Guo to lead the six armies against the Quan Rong whom King Mu had moved to Taiyuan.

According to bronze inscriptions of King Yi (夷)'s period, Zhou once sent out a force in pursuit because the Southern Huaiyi attacked inward; the inscription of the Yu gui says: "The Southern Huaiyi moved to Shu and attacked inward … [the King] ordered Yu to pursue and strike them at Shangluo." The E Hou Yufang ding and the Shi Mi gui also record King Yi (夷)'s campaigns to the south and to the east.
After King Yi (夷) of Zhou's death his son Hu succeeded; he is King Li.

div.head: c. 900–860 BC: archaeological appearances
div.p: The Xindian culture entered the late stage of its final period; the Lanqiao–Xujianian type of the Siwa culture reached its lower limit.
The Namgyeong Bronze Age Phase II culture took over from the Geumtan-ri Bronze Age Phase II culture and carried its development forward.
The Beomui-guseok Phase IV culture took over from the Beomui-guseok Phase III culture and carried its development forward.
The Songguk-ri culture area took shape.

div.head: c. 860–841 BC
div.p: King Li was without the Way; the Huaiyi came raiding, and the King ordered Guo Zhong to campaign against them, but he did not prevail. King Li was violent and cruel, and Xiong Qu, fearing that he would attack Chu, likewise gave up his title of king.

Yufang, Marquis of E, was the leader who brought the Huaiyi in on this invasion, and E therefore became the chief target of the campaign of Duke Wu, chief commander of the Zhou court; the war recorded in the Yu ding, because it ended in the capture of Yufang, dealt the Southern Huaiyi and the Dongyi a heavy and perhaps even a mortal blow.

According to the inscription of the Zongzhou zhong, a bronze of King Li's period, in the later part of the reign of King Li of the Western Zhou, Yufang, Marquis of E, had already disappeared, and Fuzi had risen in his place; the capital where Fuzi was seated was broken, and Fuzi, left with no choice, came with the states of the Nanyi and the Dongyi to have audience of King Li. With this the trouble that the Western Zhou had from the Dongyi and the Nanyi was settled for a time.

According to the Duo You ding, unearthed at Xiaquan village in Shaanxi, the Xianyun in King Li's time invaded the region around Haojing; the Zhou court sent out troops to strike back, not only to drive off the invading Rong and Di and to win back the people taken captive and the goods carried off, but, more important, to make the Rong and Di offer tribute at fixed times and to keep up the old system of the "Wild Domain".

div.head: c. 841–827 BC
div.p: The King's conduct was violent, cruel, extravagant and arrogant; the people of the capital rose in revolt and attacked King Li, and King Li fled to Zhi.

The so-called "people of the capital" (国人) are the "citizens" who lived in the capital; they had the duty of paying the military levy and of serving as soldiers, and were an important pillar of the state of the time in both politics and war; when the state was in danger, or there was some great matter such as moving the capital or deposing and setting up a ruler, those in power always had to ask their views, and they would speak their mind and even take action. At this time King Li of Zhou was violent and cruel, killed the people of the capital who spoke ill of him and forbade them to speak, and for this he was banished to Zhi by the people of the capital.

The Shiji, Basic Annals of Zhou records: "The Duke of Shao and the Duke of Zhou, the two Chancellors, conducted the government, and it was styled Gonghe", which is perhaps not accurate; the record of the old-text Bamboo Annals should be followed: "When King Li had fled, there was one He, Earl of Gong, who conducted the affairs of the Son of Heaven in his stead."

In the third year after Qin Zhong was set up, King Li of Zhou was without the Way, and some of the Lords revolted against him. The Western Rong rose against the royal house and destroyed the clan of Daluo at Quanqiu.
In the fourteenth year of Gonghe, King Li died at Zhi; the Heir Apparent Jing had grown up in the house of the Duke of Shao, and the two Chancellors then together set him up as King; he is King Xuan.

div.head: c. 827–800 BC
div.p: When King Xuan came to the throne, the two Chancellors assisted him; he put the government in order and took as his model the ways handed down from Wen, Wu, Cheng and Kang, and the Lords again acknowledged Zhou as their head. He made Qin Zhong a Grand Master to punish the Western Rong, and Qin Zhong died at it. Afterwards the Western Rong were broken, and Quanqiu was given to the descendants of Qin Zhong, who were made Grand Masters of Xichui.

The Odes, Greater Odes, Jiang Han sings of Hu, Earl of Shao, receiving King Xuan's command to campaign against the Huaiyi, winning the victory and being rewarded. The poem says: "Large was the volume of the Jiang and the Han, / And the troops advanced like a flowing current. / There was no resting, no idle wandering; / We were seeking for the tribes of the Huai. / We had sent forth our chariots; / We had displayed our falcon-banners. / There was no resting, no remissness; / Against the tribes of the Huai were we marshalled. / The king had given charge to Hu of Shao: / 'Open up the whole of the country; / Make the statutory division of my lands there … / As far as the southern sea.'"

The Odes, Greater Odes, Chang Wu sings of King Xuan commanding the Grand Preceptor Nanzhong Huangfu to take command of the six armies and march against Xu, forcing it to submit to the court. The last stanza of the poem says: "The king's plans were directed in truth and sincerity, / And the region of Xu came [at once to terms]; / Its [chiefs] were all collected together; / Through the merit of the Son of Heaven. / The country was all reduced to order; / Its [chiefs] appeared before the king. / They would not again change their minds, / And the king said, 'Let us return.'"

The Odes, Lesser Odes, Cai Qi sings of the victory won by the minister Fangshu at King Xuan's command. The poem says: "Foolish were the savage tribes of Jing, / Presuming to oppose our great region. / Fangshu is of great age, / But full of vigour were his plans. / He led his army on, / Seized [the chiefs] for the question, and made captives of a crowd [besides]. / Numerous were his war chariots, / Numerous and in grand array, / Like the clap or the roll of thunder their onset. / Intelligent and true is Fangshu. / He had gone and smitten the Xianyun, / And the tribes of Jing came, awed by his majesty."

div.head: c. 800–781 BC
div.p: King Xuan did not perform the ploughing of the sacred field at Qianmu; Duke Wen of Guo remonstrated that this would not do, but the King did not listen. Since the banishment of King Li the rite of the sacred field had lapsed, and when King Xuan came to the throne he did not go back to the ancient practice.

The ploughing of the sacred field was a tradition of the Zhou period; the farmers took part in a collective hunt, which was in the nature of military training, and so the total number of farmers could also be counted by this means. Once King Xuan "did not plough the Qianmu", the total number of farmers could no longer be counted in this way.
In the spring of the thirty-second year, King Xuan attacked Lu and set up Duke Xiao. From this time the Lords were at odds.

In the thirty-ninth year there was a battle at Qianmu, and the royal army was routed by the Rong of the Jiang clan; having lost the army of the southern states, King Xuan then numbered the people at Taiyuan.
In the forty-sixth year, King Xuan died, and his son Gongsheng, King You, was set up.

div.head: c. 800–781 BC: archaeological appearances
div.p: The Xindian culture reached its lower limit; the Shajing culture arose.

div.head: c. 780–770 BC
div.p: Ten years after King Xuan's campaign against the Shen Rong, King You ordered Boshi to attack the Rong of Liuji; the army was defeated, and Boshi died there. King You was heavily defeated in attacking the Rong, and with this the Rong peoples of the west grew stronger still.

While King You of Zhou was on the throne, the Zhou people suspected that King Xuan's sudden death while hunting had to do with the state of Zhu, and called Zhu to account; according to the Chunqiu Gongyang Zhuan, "The men of Zhulou were constantly under attack from Zhou, who said: 'Why did you bring death on our Son of Heaven?'"

The Odes, Greater Odes, Shao Min describes the state of things when drought and man-made calamity pressed together; the poem says: "Compassionate Heaven is arrayed in angry terrors; / Heaven is indeed sending down ruin, / Afflicting us with famine, / So that the people are all wandering fugitives; / In the settled regions and on the borders all is desolation. / Heaven sends down its net of crime; / Devouring insects, who weary and confuse men's minds, / Ignorant, oppressive, negligent, / Breeders of confusion, utterly perverse: / These are the men employed to tranquillize our country." "Formerly, when the former kings received the Mandate, / There were such men as the Duke of Shao, / Who in a day would open up the state a hundred li; / Now in a day the state is contracted a hundred li. / Alas, alas! / Among the men of today, / Are there not still some of the old virtue?" This is a poem of King You of Zhou's time, and its words "now in a day the state is contracted a hundred li" show that at this time the Quan Rong and the states of Shen, Zeng and others were constantly invading the territory of Zhou, and that the situation was already very pressing.

At the end of the Western Zhou, with man-made calamity and natural disaster pressing together in this way, the nobles and the people of Zhou alike sought some way to escape the great catastrophe. And so the state of Guo, in King You's time, moved east ahead of Zheng.

The Guoyu, Discourses of Zheng records Shi Bo saying at the end of the Western Zhou: "Shen, Zeng and the Western Rong are just now strong, and the royal house is just now in turmoil; if the King means to give rein to his desires at such a time, will it not be hard? The King wishes to kill the Heir Apparent so as to establish Bofu, and he is sure to demand him of Shen; the men of Shen will not give him up, and he is sure to attack them. If he attacks Shen, and Zeng and the Western Rong join together to attack Zhou, Zhou will not be held."

The Guoyu, Discourses of Jin I records that when Duke Xian divined about attacking the Li Rong, Shi Su said: "King You of Zhou attacked Bao, and the men of Bao gave him Bao Si as a wife; Bao Si won his favour and bore Bofu, and thereupon she made common cause with Guo Shifu, drove out the Heir Apparent Yijiu and set up Bofu. The Heir Apparent fled to Shen, and the men of Shen and the men of Zeng called in the Western Rong to attack Zhou, and with that Zhou fell."

The Odes, Lesser Odes, Shiyue Zhi Jiao preserves the scene at the time of King You's ruin; the maker of the poem uses it to pass judgement on those who then governed the Western Zhou and brought calamity on the state and its people: at a time of eclipse and earthquake, of rivers boiling over and mountains falling, they still joined with Bao Si in doing evil, scraping together goods and treasure and carrying them to the Central Plains to hoard.

King You deposed the Heir Apparent Yijiu and set up Bofu (Bopan), the son born of Bao Si, as Heir Apparent. The deposed Heir Apparent Yijiu fled to Western Shen. King You led an army and besieged Western Shen, and Western Shen, joined with Western Zeng and the Quan Rong, broke the royal army and killed King You at the foot of Lishan.
